title: Balfour v. Balfour
lead: An allowance promised while illness temporarily kept a wife in England became the subject of a contract suit after the marriage deteriorated. Three appellate judges agreed that the promise was not the contract she alleged, but explained that conclusion in different ways.

actors.name: Mrs. Balfour
actors.role: Wife who remained in England on medical advice and sued for the allowance

actors.name: Mr. Balfour
actors.role: Civil engineer and Ceylon government official who promised the allowance

actors.name: Sargant J.
actors.role: Trial judge who enforced the promise

actors.name: Warrington, Duke, and Atkin L.JJ.
actors.role: Appellate judges who each explained why the contract claim failed

proceedings: Sargant J. entered judgment for the wife. The Court of Appeal unanimously allowed the husband’s appeal, with separate reasons from all three judges and judgment for the husband expressly directed by Warrington.
limits: The decision concerns this allowance promise made while the couple remained amicable and expected reunion. It neither bars actual contracts between spouses nor determines the wife’s separate maintenance and alimony rights.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent primary-source audit claimed.

sections.title: Illness postponed the wife’s return
sections.cue: Begin before the marital difficulties arose.
paragraphs: The Balfours married in August 1900 and ordinarily lived together in Ceylon, where Mr. Balfour worked as a civil engineer and Director of Irrigation for the government. They came to England in November 1915 during his leave. When that leave expired in August 1916, he had to return to Ceylon. Mrs. Balfour had rheumatic arthritis, and medical advice kept her in England.

According to Mrs. Balfour, on August 8, the day her husband sailed, he gave her a £24 cheque for the rest of August and promised £30 a month until she returned. They had discussed her expenses and considered figures together. She expected him back in England within a few months. They had not agreed to separate; the difficulties between them developed afterward. His later letter suggesting that they remain apart therefore did not establish that their earlier allowance arrangement was a negotiated separation agreement.

sections.title: The allowance became a contract claim
sections.cue: Separate this suit from the wife’s other proceedings.
paragraphs: In March 1918, Mrs. Balfour began proceedings for restitution of conjugal rights. She obtained a decree nisi on July 30 and an alimony order on December 16. Her contract action, however, sought enforcement of the August 1916 monthly promise.

Sargant J., sitting as an additional King’s Bench judge, ruled for her. Because the husband already owed a duty of support, the judge understood the parties to have contracted to fix its amount. The wife’s consent supplied consideration for the promise.

The husband appealed, arguing that this temporary domestic arrangement was neither a separation agreement nor an intended legal transaction and lacked consideration. The wife answered that spouses could contract and argued that she had surrendered her power to pledge his credit for necessaries in exchange for the allowance. The authorities she invoked involved spouses living apart. The appellate judges questioned both their relevance to spouses still living amicably and whether the asserted independent right to charge his credit existed. The asserted exchange was counsel’s argument, not an established bargain.

sections.title: Warrington found no bargain to enforce
sections.cue: Explain why the wife’s assent did not prove her alleged contract.
paragraphs: Warrington L.J. accepted that spouses could make a contract of this kind. But the wife needed to show express contractual terms or circumstances necessarily implying them. She had made no express promise to accept £30 in full satisfaction of her husband’s maintenance obligation regardless of changing needs. The spouses had simply estimated amicably what would maintain her during the medically necessary absence.

The proposed implication would bind her to £30 however her needs changed and him to pay indefinitely however his circumstances changed. Ordinary domestic discussion did not support those terms. Treating it as a bargain would extend contractual enforcement throughout everyday married life. Warrington regarded the husband’s undertaking as an expression of intention and obligation of honour without a corresponding bargain by the wife.

He directed judgment for the husband because she had not proved the contract sued upon. He did not decide whether nonpayment would let her pledge his credit or obtain some other arrangement for support.

sections.title: Duke rejected the claimed consideration
paragraphs: Duke L.J. also recognized that spouses could create contractual obligations, including undertakings concerning a wife’s separate estate under the Married Women’s Property Act 1882. A genuine separation agreement could involve mutual consideration. Neither situation described the communications proved here, which arose from spouses living in amity.

Duke rejected the supposed exchange of the wife’s right to pledge her husband’s credit. The cited authorities treated her power to charge him as an agency, not the independent and irrevocable right assumed by her lawyer. Surrendering something that was not such a right supplied no consideration. Her assent to an arrangement within her husband’s discretion did not convert his domestic promise into the alleged contract. Duke also feared unrestricted litigation if ordinary reciprocal domestic promises necessarily became enforceable bargains.

sections.title: Atkin distinguished agreement from legal intention
sections.cue: Explain why even an apparent exchange might remain noncontractual.
paragraphs: Atkin L.J. emphasized that people make agreements, such as arrangements for walks or hospitality, without intending legal obligations. Domestic allowances could likewise involve reciprocal promises and something that would count as consideration between other parties, yet lack contractual force because legal consequences were not intended. His reasoning therefore did not depend entirely on Duke’s consideration analysis.

Spouses commonly vary, renew, or abandon these arrangements as personal circumstances change. Contract enforcement would permit reciprocal lawsuits over weekly allowances and their use in situations the participants had never meant courts to regulate. Atkin’s description of the home as outside the King’s writ addressed this class of promise, not a general lack of judicial authority over marriage.

The wife bore the burden of proving a contract. Neither her undisputed oral evidence nor the letters met it. The spouses anticipated reunion. They had not meant to require her to meet every possible medical expense from £30, however her illness developed, or require him to pay that amount under every circumstance.

sections.title: The contract judgment fell
sections.cue: State the result without erasing the possibility of other rights.
paragraphs: All three judges allowed the husband’s appeal. The wife’s contract judgment was reversed, with Warrington expressly calling for judgment for the husband; there was no dissent. The court did not calculate contract damages or decide the separate alimony proceedings.

The decisive setting was the amicable relationship and expected reunion when the allowance was promised. The decision left room for actual contracts between spouses. Neither later separation nor the existence of an ordinary domestic promise alone established such a contract here.
